title: 2006 Morecambe Bay helicopter crash

agencies.name: Air Accidents Investigation Branch
agencies.report_title: AAIB Special Bulletin: 1/2007 - Aerospatiale SA365N Dauphin 2, G-BLUN, 27 December 2006

location.name: Approximately 0.25 nautical miles south of North Morecambe platform, Morecambe Bay, Irish Sea

summary: A Eurocopter AS365 Dauphin helicopter operating a scheduled transit between gas platforms in Morecambe Bay crashed into the sea during an approach to North Morecambe platform on the night of 27 December 2006. During a dark night with poor weather, the co-pilot handling the helicopter became disoriented and misjudged the approach path. The co-pilot's request for assistance was not clearly articulated, and the commander's takeover was delayed approximately 4 seconds and not smooth. All seven occupants, including both flight crew, perished.
probable_cause: The co-pilot became disoriented in dark night and poor weather conditions, misjudging the approach path. The transfer of control to the commander was delayed and not smooth because the co-pilot did not articulate his need clearly and the commander was not mentally primed to assume control.

factors.evidence: The accident occurred during dark night conditions on 27 December 2006 at 1834 hrs, removing external visual references (p. 1).
Poor weather conditions with visibility between 3 to 5 nautical miles and rain reported at the time of approach (p. 1).
The co-pilot handling the helicopter became disoriented in dark night and poor weather conditions, misjudging the approach path during approach to North Morecambe platform (p. 1, 2).
The co-pilot did not articulate clearly his need for assistance; the request for help was not sufficiently explicit, hindering the commander's recognition of the need to take control (p. 1).
The commander was not mentally primed to take control of the helicopter, resulting in delayed and not smooth transfer of control approximately 4 seconds after co-pilot indicated difficulty (p. 1).
The helicopter crashed into the sea approximately 0.25 nautical miles south of North Morecambe platform with all seven occupants killed; fuselage disintegrated on impact (p. 1).

events.text: Helicopter departs Millom West platform at 1826 hrs, commencing transit to North Morecambe platform at height of 500 feet; co-pilot is handling pilot
Helicopter makes initial approach to North Morecambe platform on heading of 120°(M); approach appears normal to helideck team
During later stages of approach, helicopter slowly pitches nose down and commences slow roll to right; collective lever raised increasing power
Crew becomes unhappy with approach; co-pilot asks for assistance from commander
Commander takes control of helicopter as go-around is commenced; helicopter continues to roll to right and pitch nose down

One second after commander assumes control, helicopter attains maximum nose-down pitch attitude of 38° coincident with 38° bank angle to right; indicated airspeed 80 knots, radio altitude 300 feet, rate of descent 1,400 feet per minute

Over next 2.5 seconds, helicopter rolls level and pitch attitude reduces to 13° nose down; radio altitude 170 feet, indicated airspeed over 100 knots, rate of descent approximately 1,400 feet per minute
Over next 5.5 seconds, helicopter commences slow roll to right; pitch attitude remains relatively unchanged; indicated airspeed continues to increase
Last recorded parameters indicate radio altitude of 30 feet, 12° nose-down pitch attitude, indicated airspeed 126 knots, and angle of bank 20° to right
Helicopter crashes into the sea approximately 0.25 nautical miles south of North Morecambe platform; fuselage disintegrates on impact
Helideck team hears crash into sea; alarm raised and coastguard contacted at 1835 hrs; six bodies recovered that evening; seventh occupant remains missing

notes: Events extracted from flight progression and recorded data analysis (p. 1-2)
11 events documented with derived clock times from departure at 1826 hrs and crash at 1834 hrs (8 minutes elapsed)
Key sections read: History of Flight (p. 1), Recorded Data (p. 1-2), Engineering (p. 1), Weather (p. 1)
This is a Special Bulletin; detailed final investigation report not yet completed at time of publication
Spatial disorientation in dark night with poor weather contributed to crew coordination failure
No evidence of pre-impact mechanical malfunction; human factors were primary cause
